passages.t: The ark in its tent, and bread for everyone
passages.happening:
‘So they brought the ark of God and placed it inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And they presented burnt offerings and peace offerings before God’ (verse 1). When the sacrifices are done, David speaks God's favor over the people in the name of the LORD and gives every man and woman of Israel ‘a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake’ (verse 3).

‘David appointed some of the Levites to minister before the ark of the LORD, to celebrate, to give thanks, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel’ (verse 4). Asaph leads, with harps, lyres and cymbals, and two priests blow the trumpets regularly before the ark (verses 5-6). On that day David first commits to Asaph and his brothers a song of thanksgiving (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The ark has arrived at last. After the failure of chapter 13 and the careful procession of chapter 15, this chapter shows what the arrival is for: not one celebration but a pattern of praise that goes on day after day.

Burnt offerings were wholly burned on the altar as an act of dedication. Peace offerings were shared: part burned, part given to the priests, and part eaten by the worshipers in a meal before God. David's gift of bread and cakes to every man and woman stretched that meal to the whole people. A king who spoke God's favor over the people in the LORD's name was showing that his own rule stood under God's.

The Levites' work is named in three verbs: to celebrate, to give thanks and to praise. The word for giving thanks, yadah, means to acknowledge out loud what God is and has done; the same verb can mean to confess sin. The word for celebrate is literally to remember, zakar: in Hebrew thought remembering is active, calling the past into the present so that it shapes what people do.
passages.later: When Solomon's temple was dedicated, the trumpeters and singers ‘lifted up their voices, accompanied by trumpets, cymbals, and musical instruments, in praise to the LORD’ (2 Chronicles 5:13). The order David began here is the order that sings there. After the exile Nehemiah remembered it: ‘For long ago, in the days of David and Asaph, there were directors for the singers and for the songs of praise and thanksgiving to God’ (Nehemiah 12:46).
passages.asks: David made sure every man and woman went home with bread. Ask whether the worship you share includes the people who are easy to leave out. And ask what in your week is set apart, regularly, for giving thanks.

passages.happening:
The song opens, “Give thanks to the LORD; call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations” (verse 8). Its first part calls Israel to seek the LORD and to remember: ‘Remember His covenant forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations’ (verse 15), the covenant made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac and confirmed to Jacob, with the promise of the land of Canaan (verses 16-18). It recalls the time ‘When they were few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land’ (verse 19), wandering from nation to nation, and God protecting them (verses 20-22).

The second part widens to the whole earth: “Sing to the LORD, all the earth. Proclaim His salvation day after day” (verse 23). ‘For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens’ (verse 26). The families of the nations are called to bring an offering, and heaven, sea, fields and trees rejoice, ‘for He is coming to judge the earth’ (verse 33).

The song ends with thanks and a plea: “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 34). The people are to cry out to God to gather and deliver them from the nations, and the song closes, ‘Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting’ (verse 36), and all the people answer with Amen and praise.
passages.hearers:
The song moves in three stages: Israel remembering the covenant (verses 8-22), the whole earth called to worship (verses 23-33), and thanks with a closing prayer (verses 34-36). It is made of lines that also stand in the book of Psalms: verses 8 to 22 match Psalm 105:1-15, verses 23 to 33 match most of Psalm 96, and verses 34 to 36 match Psalm 106:1 and 106:47-48.

Scholars differ on how the two forms are related. Some think the Chronicler took psalms already sung in the second temple and joined them for this scene. Others think an older song from David's time lies behind both. Either way, the song does what the Levites were appointed to do. It remembers aloud.

Its words would have struck the Chronicler's first readers hard. They too were few in number, a small community under Persian rule, many of their people still scattered among the nations. The prayer for God to gather and deliver his people from the nations was their prayer. The key word of the refrain, chesed, translated loving devotion, is covenant love: loyal, generous kindness that keeps faith with a promised relationship. The covenant, berit, is God's sworn commitment to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the ark itself is named for it.
passages.later: The same lines open a psalm: ‘Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations’ (Psalm 105:1). The closing prayer stands in another: ‘Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise’ (Psalm 106:47).
passages.asks: The song remembers a time when God's people were few, strangers and on the move, and God kept them. Ask what you would remember aloud if you had to tell your own story as God's story. And ask what it would mean to give thanks before the prayer for rescue has been answered.

passages.t: Praise in Jerusalem, sacrifice at Gibeon
passages.happening:
‘So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to minister there regularly according to the daily requirements’ (verse 37), with Obed-edom and his relatives, and gatekeepers (verse 38).

‘And David left Zadok the priest and his fellow priests before the tabernacle of the LORD at the high place in Gibeon’ (verse 39), to offer the burnt offerings morning and evening, as the Law commanded (verse 40). With them are Heman, Jeduthun and others chosen by name to give thanks to the LORD, singing that His loving devotion endures forever (verse 41). Then the people go home, ‘and David returned home to bless his household’ (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
For a time Israel's worship stood in two places. The tabernacle made under Moses, with its bronze altar, stood at the high place of Gibeon, about six miles north-west of Jerusalem. The ark, which had once stood inside it, was now in a separate tent in Jerusalem. David staffed both: sacrifice continued at Gibeon under Zadok, and Asaph led praise before the ark. The arrangement lasted until Solomon's temple brought ark and altar together again.

The gatekeepers guarded the entrances to the holy area and controlled who came in. The refrain sung at Gibeon, that God's loving devotion endures forever, recurs through Chronicles and becomes one of Israel's central confessions.

The chapter ends quietly. After the public worship, the king goes home to speak God's favor over his own household.
passages.later: First Kings says that Solomon ‘went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place’ (1 Kings 3:4). When the foundation of the second temple was laid, the people sang, “For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever” (Ezra 3:11).
passages.asks: David went from the public worship of the nation to speak God's favor over his own household. Ask whether the faith you show in public is carried home. And ask who in your house needs to hear you give thanks.
